about.title: About Me
about.description: Senior .NET engineer moving into applied AI: I integrate LLM systems into enterprise software, and I measure them before I claim anything about them.
paragraphs: Ten years of production .NET across judicial and government systems — APIs, microservices, SSIS/ETL pipelines, SQL Server and PostgreSQL at scale, Kafka and Debezium for change data capture, Docker and Kubernetes to ship it. That is the half of AI engineering that is just engineering, and it is the half most demos skip.

The AI work is built the same way. My flagship is an Arabic legal RAG system where the question set, the reference checker and the scoreboard were written before the retriever existed. Four retrieval configurations are compared under bootstrap confidence intervals; generation is scored by a program that audits every citation against the articles the retriever actually returned, with no judge model in the loop.

It also retracted its own headline. At 15 questions dense retrieval looked best; I tripled the eval set to 60 (20 held out), re-ran it, and at 30 scored questions no ordering of the four configurations survives its confidence interval. The apparent reversal was the question mix changing, not the retrievers — re-weighting by the old mix brings dense back to the top. The README now says so, under a heading that says so.

items.title: Arabic Legal RAG — measured retrieval and citation-forced generation
items.problem: Arabic legal text breaks a RAG pipeline silently. The PDF stores text in visual order, so every word extracts reversed; Arabic-Indic digits sit inside the Arabic Unicode block, so a naive reversal turns article 25 into article 52 — a real article, wrong number, no error; and the normalisation that genuinely helps retrieval inflates the score if it is reused at evaluation time.
items.description: Article-level corpus, a hand-written question set with machine-verified article references, and four retrieval configurations compared under bootstrap confidence intervals. Generation is citation-forced and audited by a program rather than a judge model: every citation is resolved against the corpus and against the exact articles the retriever returned.

metrics.label: Reranker latency cost (7,994 vs 145 ms median; 55–64x across runs), for no gain the eval can resolve
Fabricated citations, in all 21 generation runs
Eval questions, 20 held out — enough to overturn the repo's own headline

items.limitation: 30 scored questions, and every Recall@5 interval overlaps every other (0.467–0.767 across the four configurations), so this eval set cannot order them. Generation grounds only 12 of 30 answers fully — the model omits citations rather than inventing them — and the output depends on where the model runs: deterministic at every GPU placement measured, different between them. Across five placements the pre-registered abstention check fails at 0 layers, passes at 2, 8 and 17, and fails at 34 — so it is never quoted without its layer count. The corpus also failed its fidelity check against the official gazette, so every number is performance on this corpus, not a statement about the law.

evidence.command: python evals/ablation_result.py  |  python evals/retrieval_latency.py --reps 3 --warmup 3  |  python tasks.py answer-eval --model ollama:gemma3:4b  |  python evals/generation_variance.py
evidence.commit: 4fe53a93 (quality, latency, generation) · d5379c39 · 7455aba8 · 34690455 (placement runs, pre-registered) — tag portfolio-v6
evidence.environment: Python 3.14.6, torch 2.14.0+cpu — checked by each harness, not asserted. Retrieval on CPU (i7-8750H, 6 cores / 12 threads, 15.9 GB). Generation on gemma3:4b via Ollama, Q4_K_M, greedy, temperature 0, 128-token cap.
evidence.dataset: 56 articles (Egypt Law 151/2020). 60 questions — 40 dev (30 scored, 10 abstention) and 20 held-out test the harness cannot load unless named. k=5; latency n=90.
evidence.note: Each harness refuses to describe a dirty worktree: it runs git status itself and stamps worktree_clean into its own output, so a result produced from an edited tree says so.

items.title: Intent Router — fine-tuned encoder against a prompted LLM
items.problem: Train a small classifier, or just prompt an LLM? The question usually gets answered by instinct. Here it was answered by running both over the same bilingual (Arabic/English) labelled set and measuring accuracy, latency and throughput.
items.description: A fine-tuned multilingual DistilBERT against a self-hosted LLM with schema-constrained JSON output, behind a .NET 8 Minimal API that validates and forwards to the Python service through a typed HttpClient.

metrics.label: LLM accuracy, with no training at all
Fine-tuned encoder accuracy
Encoder latency advantage per request

items.limitation: 32 held-out examples and no confidence intervals — one example is 3.1 points, so the accuracy gap is a direction, not a margin. The cost column in the repo is modelled from an assumed hourly host rate, never billed, and is labelled as such.

evidence.environment: Encoder on CPU; qwen2.5:7b-instruct through Ollama.
evidence.note: The harness records no device metadata, so the README states that the split between CPU and GPU is not in the record rather than guessing at it.

items.title: Tool Agent over MCP — a guarded loop, measured on a 3B model
items.problem: An agent that can call tools can also call the wrong ones, loop, or answer confidently past what it retrieved. The question is where a small local model breaks, measured task by task rather than assumed.
items.description: An agent loop over an MCP server (calculator, knowledge search, clock) with an allowlist, argument-schema checks, repeat-call detection and an iteration cap — plus a narrow recovery path for a model that emits tool calls as text instead of structured calls.

metrics.label: Tasks completed (4/8); every single-step task passed
Runs stopped by the iteration guardrail — both multi-step tasks among them
Confident wrong answer after a correct retrieval

items.limitation: Eight tasks: one is 12.5 points, so the pattern (single-step works, multi-step breaks) is the finding, not the rate. One model, qwen2.5-coder:3b; gemma3:4b is rejected by Ollama for tool calls outright.

evidence.environment: qwen2.5-coder:3b via Ollama, temperature 0. Windows 11, 15.9 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB (Ollama offloads part of the model).
evidence.dataset: 8 tasks (AR/EN): arithmetic, policy lookup, date, and two multi-step.
evidence.note: The harness refuses a dirty tree and stamps the commit into the result file; CI runs 89 model-free tests.

items.title: LLM Serving Cost — measured throughput against a break-even
items.problem: When does serving a model yourself beat paying per token? The usual answer compares prices and forgets to ask whether the hardware can even produce the break-even volume.
items.description: A streaming benchmark (time to first token, tokens/s, p95) over short, medium and long Arabic prompts, and a cost model that reports both the break-even volume and the monthly capacity the measured throughput can reach.

metrics.label: Local token cost vs illustrative hosted price, at measured throughput
Median time to first token once loaded, every prompt class
Break-even ~119M tokens/month vs ~25M capacity — not reachable here

items.limitation: Two small models on one laptop, single requests, no concurrency. Server cost and API prices are inputs, not measurements. Found and fixed a units bug that had put the break-even 1000x too low.

evidence.environment: Windows 11, 15.9 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB (Ollama offloads part of the model).
evidence.dataset: 24 streamed requests: 2 models x 6 prompts x 2 repetitions, no warm-up; medians reported.
evidence.note: Prices are per 1M tokens in every parameter name, pinned by a test.

items.title: .NET AI Assistant — an LLM feature inside Clean Architecture
items.problem: LLM demos live in notebooks. What does the same feature look like inside an ordinary ASP.NET Core backend — and how is it tested without the model in CI and with it for real?
items.description: ASP.NET Core 8 + MediatR: classify intent, retrieve when factual, answer through Ollama. The model and the knowledge store are ports; unit and in-process API tests replace the model, and an eval runs the real pipeline against the real model.

metrics.label: Eval checks passed with the real model (5 cases x intent + content)
Model-free unit and in-process API tests in CI
Wall clock for the model eval, including load

items.limitation: Five cases is a smoke test of the vertical slice, not a quality measurement; content checks are substring assertions after stripping Arabic diacritics, and nothing else is folded.

evidence.environment: gemma3:4b via Ollama, .NET SDK 10.0.302. Windows 11, 15.9 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB (Ollama offloads part of the model).
evidence.note: The runner parses the test host's TRX output and records the commit; it refuses a dirty tree.

items.title: LLM Observability — tracing a RAG pipeline span by span
items.problem: "The model is slow" is not a diagnosis. Where does a request actually spend its time, what does the first request cost, and can a build fail when quality drops?
items.description: A traced RAG pipeline (retrieve, rerank, generate) writing spans to a local sink, per-stage latency and token accounting, and a CI gate on thresholds fixed before the run.

metrics.label: Share of warm pipeline time spent generating
First request vs warm median — the embedding model loading, not the LLM
Quality gates passed (retrieval, grounding, abstention)

items.limitation: Twelve questions on a synthetic HR corpus: the gate proves the mechanism fails a build on regression; the rates are too small a sample to rank anything. Latency is one process on a shared desktop.

evidence.environment: gemma3:4b via Ollama; multilingual-e5-base encoder; mMARCO cross-encoder. Windows 11, 15.9 GB RAM, GTX 1050 Ti 4 GB (Ollama offloads part of the model).
evidence.dataset: 12 questions, 48 spans; every span is in the tracked traces file.
evidence.note: The gate and the dashboard share one median() — they once disagreed on the same traces.

items.title: LoRA vs full fine-tuning — a multilingual encoder on CPU
items.problem: How much of full fine-tuning does LoRA recover when it trains under 1% of the parameters — measured on the same data, seed and epochs, not taken from a paper?
items.description: Three configurations of distilbert-base-multilingual-cased on the intent-router data — classifier head only, LoRA (r=8 on attention), and full fine-tuning — trained on CPU with a fixed seed.

metrics.label: LoRA accuracy (23/32) vs 0.750 full and 0.562 head only
Parameters trained by LoRA
Saved adapter vs 541 MB full model

items.limitation: 32 eval rows: the Wilson intervals overlap, so the ordering is a direction and LoRA vs full is one question apart. The 4-bit half of QLoRA is not demonstrated — bitsandbytes needs CUDA and this torch build is CPU-only.

evidence.note: Deterministic on CPU with a fixed seed: the same numbers came out before and after the repository existed.
